meta.title: Where Should the Cut-Off Sit?
meta.summary: Under a volume need and a bad-rate appetite, the PD gate is a policy point on an acceptance frontier — not the score that maximises a pure ranking metric. Home Credit sample scorecard; OOT figures frozen and labeled.

hero.title: Where Should the Cut-Off Sit?
hero.question: Where should the PD cut-off sit under a volume / risk budget?

sections.headline: The gate is a policy choice
sections.body:
This story ships as a directed film. Open /stories/where-should-the-cutoff-sit/film.

Ranking skill (Gini) is not the same as a cut-off you can ship. The operating point maximises approval subject to a bad-rate appetite among the approved.

methodology: Directed film scrubbing a seeded application PD field. Champion scorecard and OOT cut-off metrics are frozen from PowerBI/11-credit-risk gold (LightGBM + Platt). Operating policy maximises OOT approval subject to bad rate among approved ≤ 4% appetite. Cloud marks are illustrative; published figures are calculated or observed as tagged in the evidence pack.
limitations: Sample model only — not production IRB or IFRS 9. Competition history is not a live euro-area retail book. LGD 0.45 is illustrative. Mid-50s time-OOT Gini is honest for this public feature set. Budgeted appetite is an illustrative policy input.

reader.orientation: A lender has to say yes or no to each loan application before knowing how it ends. This story follows one application into a risk score, then a whole book of them, and asks where to draw the line between yes and no, and what that line costs.

terms.definition: Here, the dataset's flag for payment difficulties: a payment more than a set number of days late on one of the loan's first instalments.
The model's estimate of the chance that this applicant defaults, from 0% to 100%.
The model currently chosen to score applications. Here it is gradient-boosted trees with a calibration step on top.
Its probabilities match what happens: of applicants given 8%, about 8 in 100 default.
The PD line: approve an application when its PD is at or below it, reject it when it is above.
The curve of approval rate against bad rate that every possible gate traces. The decision is a point on it.
The share of approved loans that go on to default.
The gate where the score best separates defaulters from the rest. A statistical choice that ignores how much bad rate the lender can carry.
The most bad rate the lender will accept among approved loans. 4% in this story, set as an illustration.
Applications from a later period than the model was built on. How the model does there is the best guide to how it will do live.
How well the score ranks defaulters above everyone else: 0% is a coin toss, 100% is perfect.
How far the mix of applicants on one input has moved since the model was built. A large value means the score may no longer fit.
How strongly one input separated defaulters from the rest when the score was built.
